title: A Young King Repairs the Temple
overview: Joash, guided by a trusted priest, gets the neglected temple in Jerusalem repaired, but later hands its treasures to a foreign king and is murdered by his own officials.

parts.label: Joash begins his reign (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Joash ruled Judah for forty years and did what pleased the LORD while Jehoiada, the priest who had protected and crowned him as a child, guided him. The wording may hint that things changed later, and local hilltop altars, used for worship outside the one temple in Jerusalem, stayed in use.

parts.label: Repairs that never happen (vv. 4-8)
parts.note: Joash told the priests to use temple income for repairs: a set payment owed by each person, payments made to fulfill vows, and free gifts. By the twenty-third year of his reign nothing had been fixed, so he took both the money and the job away from them; the text does not say why they stalled, though some think the funds went to the priests' own upkeep.

parts.label: A collection chest (vv. 9-12)
parts.note: Jehoiada set a chest with a hole in its lid beside the altar, and the priests guarding the entrance put the gifts brought to the temple into it. When it filled, the king's secretary and the high priest counted the money together and paid it straight to the work supervisors, who hired carpenters and masons and bought timber and stone.

parts.label: Money kept for its purpose (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: This money went to the workers rather than to new gold or silver temple utensils, and the supervisors were so honest that no one asked them for accounts. The priests still kept the payments linked to guilt and sin offerings, which the law assigned to them.

parts.label: Paying off an invader (vv. 17-18)
parts.note: Hazael, king of Aram (roughly modern Syria), captured the Philistine city of Gath and then turned toward Jerusalem. Joash bought him off with the sacred gifts his ancestors had dedicated and the gold from the temple and palace treasuries, the very place he had worked to restore.

parts.label: Killed by his own officials (vv. 19-21)
parts.note: Two of his officials assassinated Joash, and this chapter gives no motive. The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 24 links the killing to his later turn away from God after Jehoiada died, including his execution of Jehoiada's son.

think: When someone does good mainly because a trusted mentor is guiding them, what do you think happens to that goodness once the mentor is gone?
